Client's answers:
- Estranged from Marcos (the son) for 6 years. Does not want to leave him anything. If the law mandates it, wants to leave the minimum, with protective clauses attached.
- The management company charges 8% (admin fee on rent — deductible against PF (individual) carnê-leão (withholding) per `locacao_pf_vs_pj.md`: "comissão de administração (management commission)").
- "I pay the IPTU and condo fees on the vacant units" — IPTU and condo fees on vacant properties are borne by her. Wait: she pays IPTU/condo on vacant units — but those are the 2 owner-occupied/vacant properties (Campos do Jordão, Cotia land)? Actually "vagos" = vacant rental units. The CSV has no vacant rentals — all 9 are rented, 2 are owner-occupied/vacant. Hmm. "I pay the IPTU and condo on the vacant ones" — she pays IPTU/condo on the vacant properties (the 2 not rented: Campos do Jordão house, Cotia land — Cotia is land, no condo). These amounts are not given as numbers. So for PF rental taxation, deductible = 8% admin fee on collected rent (rent received from individuals is subject to carnê-leão; deductions: IPTU, condo paid by landlord, admin fee). Admin fee 8% × 84,900 = R$ 6,792/month deductible. IPTU/condo on vacant units — not deductible against rent? In carnê-leão, deductions are for expenses on the rented property (IPTU/condo paid by the landlord on the rented property). IPTU/condo on vacant/owner-occupied properties are generally not deductible from rental income — but I can't cite law outside the library. The library says "deduções: IPTU, condomínio pagos pelo locador, comissão de administração (deductions: IPTU, condo fees paid by landlord, admin fee)". The amounts of IPTU/condo are unknown — flag as unknown, but include 8% admin fee.

Recalculating PF IR with admin fee 8% deduction:
Monthly taxable: 84,900 − 6,792 = 78,108.
Tax = 27.5% × 78,108 − 908.73 = 21,479.70 − 908.73 = 20,570.97/month → annual 246,851.64. Effective rate: 246,851.64/1,018,800 = 24.23%.

Note: if the PJ (corporation) pays the management company, 8% becomes a PJ expense — but under Presumido (presumed-profit taxation), expenses don't reduce the tax (presumption on revenue), so admin fee doesn't reduce PJ tax but does reduce PF tax. This somewhat narrows the PF vs PJ gap. New comparison:
- PF: ≈ R$ 246,851.64/year.
- PJ cycle: same as before, R$ 153,508.48 (presumed tax on revenue; if revenue base is gross, IRRF also the same? Net distributable amount = revenue − taxes − 8% admin fee! If the management company is still paid by the company, cash available for distribution drops: monthly net = 84,900 − 10,335.97 − 6,792 = 67,772.03 → IRRF base = (67,772.03 − 50,000) × 10% = 1,777.20/month → 21,326.42/year. Total = 124,031.64 + 21,326.42 = 145,358.06. Effective 14.27%.
- PF side: admin fee already deducted → 246,851.64.
- Savings: 246,851.64 − 145,358.06 = 101,493.58/year.

Hmm, but should I model the admin fee inside the PJ? In either scenario the management company gets paid (she currently pays 8% in the PF scenario too — already deducted). In the PJ scenario, the management fee is a company expense reducing cash (not tax under Presumido). So the like-for-like comparison of total household outlay:

Scenario PF: revenue 1,018,800 − admin fee 81,504 (8% × 1,018,800) − IR 246,851.64 → net to her = 690,444.36.
Scenario PJ: revenue 1,018,800 − admin 81,504 − PJ taxes 124,031.64 − IRRF on distribution. Distributable = 1,018,800 − 81,504 − 124,031.64 = 813,264.36/year = 67,772.03/month → IRRF = 12 × 10% × 17,772.03 = 21,326.44. Net = 791,937.92.
Savings = 791,937.92 − 690,444.36 = 101,493.56 ✓ matches.

Also IPTU/condo on vacant units: unknown amount; in PF they might not be deductible (rental income deductions apply to properties generating rent — not in library; flag as unverified). In PJ they are expense but no tax impact under Presumido. So mostly neutral; flag.

Client's stance on Marcos: "if the law requires it, I want the minimum, with protective clauses." So plan: give Marcos his legitima (forced share) (50% of the estate), with protective clauses to the extent possible. Key point from the library: restrictive clauses on legitima property are prohibited unless there is just cause declared in a will (CC 1.848). So clauses attached to Marcos's legitima require "justa causa declarada no testamento (just cause declared in the will)". Does estrangement for 6 years constitute just cause? Just cause is a legal concept; the library doesn't enumerate what qualifies as just cause. Estrangement alone is probably not just cause for a restrictive clause; [unverified]. Flag: whether estrangement qualifies as just cause for restrictive clauses is unverified; courts may require more than mere estrangement (family discord) — not in library.

The "minimum possible" strategy for Marcos: he is entitled to 50% of the estate at her death. The legitima is calculated on the estate at death (donations subject to collation are accounted for). Options to minimize what Marcos actually receives (within the law):
- Use the disposable half (50%) now: donate the disposable half now to Ricardo/Paula (ITCMD on market value), keep Marcos's legitima intact. Marcos's legitima = 50% of the net estate at death (adding back donations for collation). So no matter what she does, Marcos will get at least 50% of the whole estate. She cannot legally reduce below 50% (without disinheritance/unworthiness grounds).
- Wait — nuance: the legitima base = estate at death net of debts; donations are collated to equalize. If she donates to R+P within the disposable half, Marcos keeps his half. Ultimately Marcos receives 50% of the total transferred + retained. So "minimum" = exactly 50% — R$ 9.265 mi out of R$ 18.53 mi (P1 assumption).
- What she can control: which assets Marcos receives (with protective clauses on the disposable half; on legitima property, clauses only with just cause), and structure (Marcos gets shares in the holding — with restrictive clauses? His legitima quota — on legitima without just cause not allowed, per library).
- So the honest answer: the minimum = 50%; on his share, protective clauses are not available absent a declared just cause; if she wants clauses on his portion, a will declaring just cause is needed, and whether estrangement qualifies is [outside library — unverified risk].
- Also, she could give Marcos his legitima in the least liquid/least desired assets (e.g., specific properties), while R+P keep control via the majority of shares — but if Marcos receives 50% of the shares → he is a 50% co-owner of the holding → blocks management (Ltda deadlock). Structure: donation of quotas in a form that gives Marcos 50% of value but non-voting (preferential quotas)? The library says nothing about voting/non-voting shares or bylaws clauses — [unverified mechanism]. Hmm, be careful: the library is the only authority; the CC excerpt does not cover quota classes. Should I even propose that? I can mention as an unverified mechanism that must be checked against law outside the library. Better approach: flag the deadlock risk itself as a library-grounded consequence? Deadlock risk is a factual/practical consequence, not legal citation — acceptable as practice note flagged as unverified (no statutory citation).
- Usufruct reservation (reserva de usufruto): she keeps control (voting rights? administration) — usufruct over quotas: library confirms ITCMD treatment; governance effects (usufructuary voting rights) are outside library — flag.
- Disinheritance (deserdação): client has not presented facts beyond estrangement → legal cause not apparent; library doesn't enumerate causes → cannot advise; if facts existed (art. 1.961 causes, outside library), she should say so. She says she has no additional info → flag as remaining unknown.

So the updated recommendations for Marcos: plan on giving Marcos the legitima (50% ≈ R$ 9.265 mi), as soon as possible:
Option A (cheapest ITCMD, equal donation): donate quotas to all 3 equally now: ITCMD 4% × market (R$ 657,200 / 577,200 if only 9 rented). Marcos gets 1/3 of quotas = his legitima? Wait — equal donation of all quotas: each receives 1/3 of R$ 16.43 mi = 5.477 mi; Marcos's legitima = 50% of the estate (18.53 mi = 9.265 mi). If she donates everything, estate = 0 but collation fiction adds donations back: Marcos's legitima = 50% of the total = 9.265 mi; his share would be 1/3 = 6.14 mi < 9.265 mi → he can claim supplementary partition (suprimento)! Important: even a donation equally to all 3 children does not cover his legitima — because she retains the disposable half for R+P. If she wants to fully resolve succession without future claims: Marcos must receive 50% (9.265 mi) of the total. That is, give Marcos more than a third: e.g., donate to Marcos quotas worth 9.265 mi (50%), Ricardo and Paula each 3.1325 mi? No wait — disposable half = 9.265 mi can be given to R+P. Marcos's legitima = 9.265 mi. If she donates Marcos 50% of quota value now, and R+P… they also receive their legitima shares of 9.265 mi (4.6325 each) + split the disposable (another 4.6325 each). If she donates everything now: Marcos must receive at least 9.265 mi worth (50% of quotas) and R+P get the rest (R 31.25% + P 31.25% with equal treatment? No: legitima gives them 25% each; the disposable 50% can be allocated freely — she can give the entire disposable to one. So quota split: Marcos 50%, Ricardo 50%, Paula 0% — permitted! Because Paula's legitima (25%) is… no wait: if Marcos gets 50% and Ricardo 50%, Paula gets 0% < her legitima 25% → Paula can claim supplement. As long as everyone receives at least 25% (their legitima share), the distribution of quotas can be: Marcos 50%, Ricardo 25% + disposable 25% = 50%, 0? She wants to favor R+P, disfavor Marcos: the constraint is Marcos ≥ 50% of the whole? No! Marcos's legitima = 50% of the whole — each child's legitima is 1/3 of half = 1/6 of the whole ≈ 3.088 mi = 16.67%. Marcos's legitima is one third of the half = 16.67% of the estate, not 50%!

Wait. Legitima = half of the estate belongs to all necessary heirs collectively; each child's individual legitima share = half ÷ number of children = 1/6 of the estate. I confused myself: the "legitima" as a class is 50%; Marcos individually is entitled to 1/3 of that = 16.67% (≈ R$ 3.088 mi). If she completely disinherits Marcos ("não recebe nada (receives nothing)"): is a donation of everything to R+P inofficious (inoficiosa)? Inofficious is measured per donee against that donee's legitima? Donation from ascendant to descendant = advance on legitima (collation). If Marcos gets nothing in life: at death, estate = 0, collation fiction: collated donations = 18.53 mi… Actual collation: heirs who received advances must bring them back to the partition in kind (art. 2002: "os herdeiros necessários que receberam doações devem conferi-las (necessary heirs who received donations must collate them)"). With 3 children, each entitled to 1/3 of the legitima half (50%): each child receives at minimum 1/6 of the estate. R+P received 18.53 in life; in the collation fiction, estate mass = 18.53; legitima half 9.265 → each child must get 3.088 in the mass; Marcos has 0 → Marcos has right to 3.088 (or up to…). And R+P's advances (9.265 each) exceed their legitima shares (3.088 each); the excess can only come from the disposable portion: disposable half 9.265 — R+P together received 18.53 = legitima 6.176 + 12.354 from the disposable, but disposable = 9.265 → excess 3.088 → reduction of Marcos's legitima → Marcos can claim 3.088 (in cash/value). Same conclusion: Marcos's minimum = 1/6 of 18.53 ≈ R$ 3.088 mi (= 16.67%). My earlier JSON field "parcela_indisponivel_pct": 50 is correct (the legitima class = 50%), and "marcos minimum" = 50%/3 = 16.67% ≈ R$ 3.088 mi.

Good — correcting the narrative in my parecer: I wrote "Marcos tem direito a 50% do acervo ≈ 9.265 mi" — wrong at the individual level! Each child's legitima = 1/6 of the estate (≈ 3.088 mi) (in the 3-children, no-spouse case). STATUS.md also repeats "Marcos's legitima = 50% of the estate (≈ R$ 9.265 mi)". Needs fixing: the unavailable half (50%) belongs to the 3 children jointly; Marcos's individual legitima = 1/3 of the half ≈ 16.67% ≈ R$ 3.088 mi.

So "se a lei obriga, quero o mínimo possível (if the law compels it, I want the minimum)": Marcos's legal minimum = his legitima = 1/6 of the estate mass at death ≈ R$ 3.088 mi (P1). Strategy: give Marcos exactly his legitima as soon as possible — ITCMD on that is 4% × 3.088 mi ≈ 123.5 thousand; the rest to R+P within legitima + disposable; nothing exceeds → no reduction, no collation dispute.

Donation plan (all in life, ITCMD 4% total on market regardless of allocation):
- Total quotas = 16.43 mi (or 14.43 mi if 9 rented). Estate for legitima calculation includes future-application (2.1 mi) too. If she donates only quotas now (14.43), Marcos receives quota worth 3.088? Note: legitima is calculated at death; if she keeps 2.1 mi + 2 owner-occupied properties (2 mi) until death, her estate at death = 4.1 mi; his legitima claim on estate = 1/6 × (4.1 + donated 14.43 = collation mass 18.53) = 3.088 — donations are collated, so his share can be satisfied from the quota already given. If she gives Marcos now quotas worth exactly 3.088 mi + he inherits the estate (4.1 mi) (his 1/3 of… no — the estate at death 4.1: legitima half 2.05 → each child 0.683; Marcos already has donated 3.088 > his total legitima 3.088… let me do the collation correctly: mass = estate 4.1 + donations 14.43 = 18.53. Each child's legitima = 3.088. Marcos's gift 3.088 = exactly his legitima → he gets no further quota claim; R+P's gifts total 11.34, their legitima 3.088 each = 6.176; excess 5.164 charged to the disposable 9.265 ✓ no inofficious donation. At death, estate 4.1: legitima 2.05 vs Marcos's advance 3.088 — he's already beyond legitima… in collation, heirs who received advance beyond legitima can keep the excess (within disposable). R+P also advanced. Estate 4.1 to be split: legitima accounting already satisfied (Marcos 3.088 + others) — disposable 9.265 vs advances charged to disposable 5.164 + 4.1 still in estate… estate 4.1 falls into the remainder of the disposable → she can will it to whoever, or intestate → split among the 3. No problem — plan works without reduction.

So the concrete answer to "minimum": Marcos's minimum = 1/6 of total ≈ R$ 3.088.000 (under P1). Give him exactly that now as quota bare-ownership (nua-propriedade) + her usufruct → ITCMD 4% × 3.088 mi ≈ R$ 123.520 on his slice; total ITCMD for all donations same as before if all donated (657/577k) — allocation is Marcos 3.088/14.43 of 577.200 ≈ 123.5 thousand, R+P the rest (453.7 thousand).

Cláusulas (clauses) on Marcos's slice: on legitima → per library, prohibited unless just cause declared in will. Estrangement ≠ obviously just cause — unverified. So: on Marcos's share (legitima), clauses probably cannot be imposed without a will + just cause [risk of invalidity]. If she wants clauses on him: put him slightly above the minimum (into the disposable portion) and impose clauses on the excess… clauses attach to the donation; she can give Marcos 3.088 (legitima, no clause) + additional within disposable with clauses. Hmm — she wants the minimum for him. Then protective clauses on his slice are largely unavailable — tell her straight: legal minimum cannot be tied with clauses without just cause in a will (art. 1.848); estrangement for 6 years, per library's citation, is not shown to be just cause — just-cause standard not in library [unverified].

On her side: usufruct reservation to keep control/income until death — library-supported for ITCMD purposes; governance effect [unverified mechanism, flag].

Also the new data: admin 8%, IPTU/condo on vacant units paid by her.
- PF recalc: admin fee deductible (library lists "comissão de administração"): monthly base = 84,900 × 0.92 = 78,108 → IR = 27.5%×78,108 − 908.73 = 20,570.97/month → 246,851.64/year (effective 24.23%). IPTU/condo on vacant units: deductibility of non-rented properties is [unverified — library's deduction refers to paid IPTU/condo, arguably on rented properties; amount unknown anyway] → excluded, flag.
- PJ: admin fee becomes company expense → cash distributable = 67,772.03/month → IRRF = 10% × 17,772.03 = 1,777.20/month = 21,326.44/year → total 145,358.08 → effective 14.27%.
- Savings = 246,851.64 − 145,358.08 = 101,493.56/year → ITBI payback 432,900/101,494 = 4.26 years; 492,900 → 4.86.

Under Presumido the admin fee doesn't reduce PJ tax (on revenue base) but does reduce PF tax — the 8% cost of management company is neutral, except for PF deduction: 8% deduction saves 27.5% × 81,504 = 22,413.60/year of PF tax. So savings narrow from ~115.7k to ~101.5k.

Alternative: terminate the 8% admin fee after PJ? Out of scope; note the admin fee reduces PF tax, slightly narrows the advantage.
